title: Constraint Integer Programming
contribution: Defines constraint integer programming (CIP) as a model class generalising CP(FD) and MIP, builds SCIP to solve it with CP, SAT and MIP integrated on one search tree, contributes reliability/inference/hybrid branching, the product score, hybrid node selection, root restarts and conflict analysis for MIP, measures each component in a 28,060-run study, and applies CIP to chip property checking.
problem_entry: Three entries: a wish to integrate IP and CP beyond the scope of SIP (p. 9), a free near-state-of-the-art platform for academics (p. 73), and chip verification where SAT fails on arithmetic and word-level IP/CP fails on control logic (p. 201); stated as the CIP model class (Def. 1.6, p. 27; Prop. 1.7, p. 28); Part II chapters enter via unmeasured common rules or SAT techniques MIP lacked (pp. 76, 174, 179).
key_idea: Low-level integration of CP, SAT and MIP on one search tree, organised around constraint handlers (pp. 16, 37-38); incumbents written as settings of one parameterised rule (reliability branching with eta_rel 0/1/inf, hybrid branching; pp. 79-83, Fig. 5.2 p. 82); product score (p. 76); conflict analysis seeded by relaxing local bounds along the dual ray (Algs. 11.1-11.2, pp. 189, 191); one constraint handler per RTL operator (pp. 202, 209).
assumptions: MILP min c^T x s.t. Ax <= b with bounds outside the matrix and specialised linear handlers (pp. 25, 74); 244 instances in ten public sets (Table A.1, p. 334), results read through class structure such as artificial or missing objectives (pp. 84, 96, 113, 126); correctness conditions for continuous and non-binary conflicts and local cuts (pp. 187, 191-192); chip CSP with register domains, free initial state, OneSpin circuits (pp. 201, 203, 337).
proof_devices: exchange argument for the optimality of best-first search (Prop. 6.1, p. 89)
characterisations of bound and interval consistency (Prop. 7.2 and Cor. 7.3, pp. 98-99)
NP-completeness by reduction from subset sum (Prop. 7.4, p. 100)
NP-hardness of the minimum bound-IIS by reduction from the minimum IIS (Prop. 11.5, p. 188)
Farkas/dual-ray proof (11.13) kept valid while bounds are relaxed (p. 188; Algs. 11.1-11.2, pp. 189, 191)
termination of term normalisation by a well-founded ordering and Dershowitz's recursive path ordering (Thm. 14.21 and Prop. 14.22, p. 236; Prop. 15.7, p. 298)
experiments: 575 public instances reduced to 244 by a five-step rule (p. 334); 244 x 115 settings = 28,060 runs with SCIP 0.90f/0.90i and Cplex 10.0.1 as LP solver, 1 h / 2 h limits, 1.5 GB (pp. 16, 333); shifted geometric mean % change vs default with single-class sets as pseudo-instances (pp. 335-336); knock-out, all off/one off/one on for cuts (p. 125), gap targets for heuristics (pp. 143-146); single runs, no seeds (p. 333); baselines Cplex 10.0.1 (pp. 334, 391) and MiniSat 2.0 (pp. 313, 317).
positioning: Differs from Coupe, Scil and Simpl in level of integration (pp. 15-16) and from DPLL(T)/HDPLL by an LP at every node (p. 202); builds on SIP, Linderoth-Savelsbergh, Bixby et al. 2000, Savelsbergh, Balas-Ceria-Cornuejols and Andreello-Caprara-Fischetti (pp. 20, 37, 62, 75, 85, 97, 125, 147); scoped disagreements with data (pp. 83, 127, 175-176); hedged novelty and named independent work (pp. 85, 98, 140-141, 179).
writing: Every Part II chapter ends with experiments in one table layout, positive values = deterioration (pp. 16, 83, 93, 126); one headline number per chapter in the introduction (pp. 16-19); hedged explanations and claims without a table labelled (pp. 69, 88, 93, 154, 191); losing defaults and refuted impressions printed (pp. 96, 114, 127, 177); minor inconsistencies (pp. 15-16, 20, 68, 340); reading guide and chapter credits (pp. 75, 115, 132, 199, 209).
limits_future: SCIP 0.90f 115 % and 0.90i 63 % slower than Cplex (p. 391), leaf-queue bottleneck (p. 94), extra LP for strong-branching conflicts (pp. 194-195), single runs and time-out bias (p. 333); open: delayed-restart criteria (p. 177), child-selection epsilon (p. 96), hybrid node-selection omega (p. 94), weakness of linearised bound disjunctions (p. 191), conflict management (p. 195), SAT-then-CIP portfolio (p. 322).

method_links.note: Knock-out from the default in thesis form: shifted-geometric-mean ratios with faster/slower counts and equal/different-path blocks; all off / one off / one on for cuts after Bixby et al.; non-additivity read as overlap; indirect effects of heuristics; time-outs scored at the limit with the bias stated
Conflict analysis is measured by adding it to a reference that lacks it, which Appendix B labels 'default'; so in the SCIP 0.90f MIP benchmarks conflict analysis was off by default
Example A.1 gives -27 % for the geometric mean (improvement for B) and +6 % and +89 % deteriorations for the shifted geometric and arithmetic means; SKILL.md reverses these signs

A proxy is not a payoff: full strong branching smallest trees but ~100 % slower; local cuts -70 % nodes, +137 % time; bound-exceeding/full conflict analysis cut nodes but not time; keeping conflicts longer on alu -25 % nodes, +37 % time; tuned Gomory cuts lost time; budgets set in solver units
The thesis does not split time into base, switching and component time (ZR 05-19 form); it reads overhead from whether node and time changes move together

Wording of SKILL.md's evidence: 'propagation only, <= 10 per infeasible subproblem, aging' are the experiment settings, not a stated default; the best variant (prop/inflp/age, -12 % time) is measured against no conflict analysis; the reason against LP cuts for non-binary conflicts is only partly given (system (11.15) 'probably very weak', not verified)

Incumbents nested in one family: eta_rel at 0, 1, inf with d, lambda, gamma, kappa; reliability branching is the hybrid with zero weights; five mu values vs the product score (best mu = 1/6 still 14 % slower); weighted node selection with omega and hybrid child selection; parameter tied to an iteration budget. The (nodes, time) knee plot of ZR 04-13 is not in the thesis, which tabulates the rules (p. 83)

Do-no-harm default: hybrid branching keeps inference branching's gains on alu and acc and equals reliability branching elsewhere; per-call guards make RENS, restarts and reduced-cost bounds no-ops when unlikely to pay
No class detector: the default is decided on the pseudo-instance-weighted total, so cuts stay on although they slow enlight and alu; the matrix-detector form appears later (ZR 09-38)

Instrument first: two years of code before research, built on SIP's source; SCIP begun October 2002; test set chosen with frozen SCIP 0.82d and Cplex 10.0.1, final runs with 0.90f; versions on request, full tables and logs on the web; leak detection in the memory-management debugging mode

Import at the data-structure level: Novikov's primer, watched literals days later, conflict analysis generalised after three weeks; watched-literal replacement re-decided by test; restarts doubted structurally and kept only after the root, delayed restarts failed; conflict analysis re-derived for LPs and general integers; VSIDS as a score; SAT restarts replaced by a jump to a best node every 100 DFS nodes; an independent discovery named

SAT restarts doubted because MIP would lose warm-start bases / LP work
features and results stamped with SCIP versions (0.82d, 0.90f, 0.90i)
CIP proves valid properties faster, SAT finds counter-examples faster; a SAT-then-CIP portfolio named

transferable: State once in a footnote what the percentages mean, and use one summary-table layout in every chapter: time on top, nodes below, positive values worse (pp. 16, 83).
In the shifted-geometric-mean total (shift 10 s for time, 100 for nodes), count each single-class test set as three pseudo-instances, so that no class dominates (pp. 335–336).
Select the test set by a written rule, run with a frozen older version and a reference solver, and list where each set comes from (pp. 333–334).
Score time-outs at the limit, and memory-outs as time-outs with the node count scaled by the nodes-per-second ratio; say that this favours the failing runs (p. 333).
Add counts of instances at least 10 % faster or slower, and equal/different-path blocks, to every detailed table (p. 339).
For interacting families, run all off, one off and one on alone, and compare the sum of the single knock-outs with all off as a measure of overlap (pp. 125–127, 142).
Report heuristics at gap targets as well as in time to optimality (pp. 143–146).
Draw the parameter interrelation diagram that shows the old rules as corners of the new one (Fig. 5.2, p. 82).
Tie the reliability parameter to a strong-branching iteration budget: at most ½ γ̂_LP + 100,000 iterations, with η_rel decreasing linearly from 8 to 1, then to 0 (pp. 79–80).
Use the product score max{q−, ε}·max{q+, ε} with ε = 10⁻⁶, tested against the weighted sum at several values of µ (pp. 76, 85).
In propagation, round new bounds within the feasibility tolerance and accept only bound changes of a minimum relative size (7.2 and 7.3, pp. 100–101).
Seed the conflict graph by relaxing bounds along the dual ray (Alg. 11.1, p. 189). Move non-binary bound changes to the conflict side to keep set-covering conflicts (p. 192).
Prefilter pairwise constraint comparisons with 64-bit signatures (p. 154).
When a published recommendation fails in your code, limit your claim to your code and test sets, and offer a mechanism (pp. 175–176).
Print refuted impressions and losing defaults next to the table that refutes them (pp. 96, 114, 127).
When a variant fails, read the logs, explain the failure, and say what would be needed instead (delayed restarts, p. 177).
